title: My Father In Law Spent Nineteen Years Restoring A Candy Apple Red 1967 Mustang He Called Penny, But After His Stroke My Brother In Law Offered To Keep It Safe In His Garage, And When Walt Finally Asked To See It We Learned It Had Sold At An
excerpt: My father-in-law, Walt Kowalczyk, bought a rusted-out 1967 Ford Mustang coupe in 1998 for nine hundred dollars. It had been sitting in a farmer’s barn outside Toledo, Ohio, for twenty years, with a family of raccoons living in the back seat.
author: admin

blocks.text: PART 1 — PENNY

My father-in-law, Walt Kowalczyk, bought a rusted-out 1967 Ford Mustang coupe in 1998 for nine hundred dollars. It had been sitting in a farmer’s barn outside Toledo, Ohio, for twenty years, with a family of raccoons living in the back seat.
Everyone told him he was crazy. My mother-in-law, Barbara, told him he was crazy. His sons told him he was crazy. Walt bought it anyway.

He spent the next nineteen years restoring it in his garage. Every evening after work, every weekend, every vacation day. He was a tool and die maker at an auto parts plant, and he could build anything. He rebuilt the engine himself. He rebuilt the transmission. He hunted down original parts at swap meets across the Midwest. He stripped the body to bare metal and painted it himself, in candy apple red, in a homemade paint booth he built out of plastic sheeting and box fans.
He did every bolt himself. He named her Penny, after the nine hundred pennies he figured he’d saved for every year of her life.

When Penny was finally finished in 2017, Walt took Barbara for a ride along the Maumee River at sunset. She cried. She told me later it was the most romantic thing he ever did, and that included their wedding.
Barbara died in 2020. After that, Penny became even more precious to Walt. He’d sit in the driver’s seat in the garage sometimes, not going anywhere, just sitting.
I married Walt’s younger son, Mike, in 2005. I’m Andrea. I’m forty-eight. I’m an office manager at a veterinary clinic. Walt has been like a second father to me for twenty years.
Walt’s older son, Rick, is fifty-four. He lives about thirty minutes away. He and Mike have never been especially close.
He did every bolt himself. He named her Penny.
PART 2 — THE STROKE
Two years ago, in March, Walt had a stroke.
He was seventy-seven. He collapsed in his garage, next to Penny. A neighbor heard his dog barking and found him on the floor. He was rushed to the hospital in Toledo.

It was a bad one. A stroke on the left side of his brain, which meant the right side of his body was affected. For weeks, he couldn’t move his right arm or his right hand at all. He couldn’t speak clearly. He spent nine days in the intensive care unit and then six weeks in a rehabilitation hospital.
Mike and I were at the hospital every day. So was Rick, at first.

While Walt was in the ICU, Rick brought up the car. He said Walt’s house would be empty for a long time. He said Penny was too valuable to leave sitting in an empty garage. Someone might steal her. He offered to “keep Penny safe” in his own garage until Walt was better.
Mike didn’t love the idea, but it made sense. Walt’s garage wasn’t very secure. Rick’s was attached to his house. We said okay.
Rick picked up Penny on a trailer while Walt was still in the hospital.

Walt worked harder in rehab than I’ve ever seen anyone work at anything. He learned to walk again, with a cane. He learned to talk again, slowly. He learned to write with his left hand, because his right hand still doesn’t work well. It took him eighteen months.
Every week, at every therapy session, he’d say the same thing. “When I can walk, I’m going to drive Penny again.”

Mike and I took turns sitting with him in the evenings. Some nights, Walt would ask about Penny in his slow, slurred voice. “Is she covered?” he’d ask. “Battery tender on?” Rick would tell him yes, she was fine, sleeping under a cover in his garage. Walt would nod and close his eyes, relieved.
When I can walk, I’m going to drive Penny again.
PART 3 — THREE WEEKS OF EXCUSES
Last month, Walt finally felt strong enough. He asked Mike to drive him over to Rick’s house so he could see his car.
Mike called Rick to set it up. Rick said it wasn’t a good time. He said his garage was a mess. He said he’d call back.
Mike called again a few days later. Rick said the car was “under a cover” and he didn’t want to disturb it. He said Walt shouldn’t be getting excited, with his heart. He said maybe next month.
Walt called Rick himself. Rick didn’t pick up.
For three weeks, Rick made excuses. His wife was sick. He was traveling for work. The garage door was broken.
Walt got quieter and quieter. He’d sit in his recliner and look out the window at his own empty garage. I knew he was starting to suspect something. I think we all were. Nobody wanted to say it.
Finally, on a Saturday afternoon, Mike said, “That’s enough.” He got in his truck and drove to Rick’s house without calling.
Rick wasn’t home. His wife, Donna, answered the door. She looked surprised, then nervous.
Donna hesitated for a long time. Then she said, “Mike, you should probably talk to Rick.” But she opened the garage door anyway.
The garage was empty. No Mustang. No car cover. Just a clean concrete floor, an oil stain, and a pile of cardboard boxes in the corner.
Mike called me from the driveway. He was so angry he could barely speak.
The garage was empty. No Mustang. No car cover. Just a clean concrete floor.
PART 4 — HE GAVE IT TO ME
Rick finally called Mike that night. He sounded defensive.

He said Walt had “given him the car.” He said that before the stroke, Walt had told him he wanted Rick to have Penny someday. He said that after the stroke, he’d needed money to pay some bills. He said he figured Dad would understand. He said he sold it.
“You sold it?” Mike said. “To who? For how much?”
Rick wouldn’t say. He said it was his business. He said it was his car now.
Mike told him that Walt had never given him anything. Rick hung up.
That night, Mike and I sat at our kitchen table and went online. We searched for 1967 Ford Mustangs in candy apple red that had sold recently. It didn’t take long.

A classic car auction company in Scottsdale, Arizona, had sold a 1967 Mustang coupe at its winter auction, the previous January. The listing was still online, with photos. Candy apple red. Original engine, rebuilt. Restored over “nineteen years by a meticulous owner.” The photos showed the interior. The white leather seats Walt had reupholstered himself. The little Saint Christopher medal Barbara had clipped to the sun visor in 2017.
The final sale price was seventy-one thousand dollars.
Mike stared at the photos for a long time. Then he said, “Dad doesn’t know yet.”
“I know,” Mike said. “I just don’t know how to tell him.”
In the end, we didn’t have to. When we got to Walt’s house the next morning, he took one look at Mike’s face and said, “It’s gone, isn’t it?”

I scrolled through the auction photos three times. There was Walt’s hand-built dashboard. There were the chrome bumpers he’d polished every Sunday afternoon. There was even a close-up of the little dent in the glove box door where Barbara had once slammed it shut during an argument about directions. Walt never fixed that dent. He said it was part of the car’s history.
It’s gone, isn’t it?
PART 5 — THE TITLE

Walt didn’t say anything for a long time after Mike told him. He just sat in his recliner and looked at his hands. His left hand, which works. And his right hand, which still curls a little and shakes when he tries to hold a cup.
Then he said, slowly, in his careful, post-stroke way of speaking, “I never gave Rick that car.”

Something about the way he said it made me think. To sell a car in Ohio, you have to transfer the title. The owner has to sign the title over to the buyer, and in Ohio, the signature has to be notarized. Then the title is filed with the county clerk of courts. Rick couldn’t have sold Penny at an auction unless the title was in his name, or unless Walt’s signature was on the transfer.
The next morning, I called the Lucas County Clerk of Courts title office. I explained the situation. I asked if they could tell me who the title for Walt’s Mustang was transferred to, and when.

The clerk was very helpful. She said that because Walt was the original owner, he was entitled to request a copy of the title history. I brought Walt in that afternoon, with his ID. He signed the request with his left hand.
The clerk printed it out and handed it to us.
The title had been transferred from Walter J. Kowalczyk to Richard W. Kowalczyk. There was Walt’s signature on the seller’s line. A notary’s stamp. And a date.
I looked at Walt. He looked at the date.
